short: A teenage peasant turned the Hundred Years' War, then burned for it.
full:
Born about 1412 to a farming family at Domremy in eastern France, Joan said from her teens that the voices of saints were instructing her to drive the English out of France. In 1429, with the Hundred Years' War going badly for the Valois cause, she persuaded the uncrowned dauphin Charles to send her to besieged Orleans. The siege was lifted on 8 May, nine days after she arrived; the English were beaten at Patay in June, and Charles was crowned at Reims in July.

Captured at Compiegne in May 1430 by Burgundian troops and sold to the English, she was tried for heresy at Rouen by a church court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned at the stake on 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen. A rehabilitation trial annulled the verdict in 1456. She was canonised in 1920 and became a patron saint of France and a national symbol claimed by every part of its politics. Sabaton's "Maid of Steel", from Legends (2025), is about her.
